summary: Explains how Differentiated Services interacts with real-time communication such as RTP-based conferencing and WebRTC. Diffserv marks packets with codepoints so network nodes can treat them differently, and the memo discusses what that means for real-time traffic.

plainLanguage.summary: Diffserv markings can change how routers forward real-time packets. RFC 7657 explains how those differences can reorder traffic and gives guidance for marking packets safely.

subtitle: How Differentiated Services markings affect real-time communication

tldr.problem: Real-time applications can send several kinds of traffic over one network flow. Different Diffserv markings may send packets through different queues, causing reordering and complicating transport congestion control.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC explains how Diffserv Codepoints select per-hop behaviors and gives guidance for using them with RTP, RTCP, TCP, SCTP, DCCP, UDP, and UDP-Lite.
tldr.outcome: The memo recommends limiting DSCP variation within transports that rely on ordering or shared congestion control, and warns that networks may change markings.

facts.label: Core PHBs discussed
facts.value: Default Forwarding, Assured Forwarding, Expedited Forwarding

today: RFC 7657 is an Informational memo and the batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It describes interactions between Diffserv and real-time communication rather than specifying a new protocol.

sections.title: Real-Time Traffic and Multiplexing
sections.content:
Real-time communication can carry audio, video, text, and data at the same time. The Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP) carries media, and applications may combine several streams, control traffic, and other protocols over one transport flow.

WebRTC and conferencing applications may use Session Description Protocol (SDP) bundle negotiation to send multiple streams over one network 5-tuple. The RFC examines what happens when packets in that shared flow use different Diffserv markings.
sections.plainLanguage: A call can send several kinds of traffic at once, sometimes through one network flow. Different handling for packets in that flow can affect how they arrive.

sections.title: Diffserv Codepoints and Forwarding Behavior
sections.content:
Differentiated Services (Diffserv) marks packets with a Diffserv Codepoint (DSCP) in the IP header. A network node maps the DSCP to a per-hop behavior (PHB), which describes the forwarding treatment for those packets. The Default Forwarding PHB provides best-effort service; Assured Forwarding (AF) defines classes with different drop precedence; Expedited Forwarding (EF) is intended for inelastic traffic.

Networks can change or remove DSCP markings at their boundaries or within a network. A sender therefore cannot rely on a DSCP being preserved end to end, or on every network offering the requested PHB.
sections.plainLanguage: A DSCP is a mark in an IP packet that helps a network choose how to forward it. A network may change that mark, and different networks may treat it differently.

sections.title: Reordering and Transport Protocols
sections.content:
Different DSCPs can select different forwarding resources, such as queues, so packets in one 5-tuple may arrive out of order. Reliable transports such as TCP and SCTP can interpret reordering as loss and trigger retransmission. Congestion-controlled transports can also respond to loss across a whole connection or association, even when different marked traffic used different resources.

RFC 7657 identifies use of multiple PHBs within one Assured Forwarding class as the main case that does not enable reordering within a 5-tuple. UDP and UDP-Lite do not themselves provide reliable delivery or congestion control, but when they carry other protocols, the encapsulated protocols remain sensitive to reordering.
sections.plainLanguage: Different packet queues can change packet order. That can look like loss to reliable transports, even when packets were only delayed relative to one another.

sections.title: Guidance for Marking Real-Time Traffic
sections.content:
For a single RTP stream, applications SHOULD use DSCPs whose PHBs do not enable reordering. RTCP packets SHOULD use a DSCP used by the associated RTP stream. A reliable transport session, SCTP association, or DCCP connection SHOULD use one DSCP for all its packets.

Different DSCPs may be used within one UDP or UDP-Lite 5-tuple, subject to the other guidance, but the service differentiation is unreliable because networks may remark the packets. Applications cannot rely on end-to-end DSCP preservation to identify frame types or other details.
sections.plainLanguage: Use one DSCP for traffic governed by one reliable transport or congestion controller. Do not rely on the far end receiving the same DSCP that the sender chose.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Effects
sections.content:
When several protocols share one UDP 5-tuple, firewalls and monitoring systems may not be able to apply policy to each protocol separately. Using several DSCPs that enable reordering also exposes the communication to more forwarding resources, which can increase exposure to resource failure or depletion.

DSCP markings are visible in the IP header. Combined with packet size and timing, they may reveal information about encrypted traffic, such as the type of media stream. The RFC refers to the security considerations of RTP and Diffserv for the underlying technologies.
sections.plainLanguage: Visible DSCP markings can reveal how encrypted traffic is grouped or treated. Shared flows can also make it harder for network security tools to inspect each protocol separately.
